prize_parts.citation: for a visionary body of prose and poetry that turns memory, the body and dream into large-scale metaphysical architectures of the novel.

statement.case_for: My opening preference for Cărtărescu holds after reading colleagues' arguments. On public knowledge, the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid show a voice that is hard to confuse with anyone else's: long-breathed, densely patterned syntax and an imagery that treats inner experience as a cosmology. Formal ambition appears sustained across very large structures rather than resting on one breakthrough book. The work belongs to a recognizable European visionary and modernist lineage while remaining its own project. The poetry as formative ground and the later novels as consolidation give a coherent oeuvre with a clear single-writer citation scope. Judged by voice, formal and linguistic achievement, imaginative depth and sustained quality, this is where I find the strongest combined case among the shortlisted entries. That judgment is provisional and rests on translations and public knowledge.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that I cannot verify how much of the effect belongs to the Romanian original and how much survives translation. Very long, recursive, self-referential books may also be unevenly sustained, with passages of obsessive density that a committee reading in translation cannot test fully. Carson's formal invention and Adonis's remaking of a poetic language are arguably more demonstrable on formal grounds, and Adonis's case is the harder one to assess in translation. If the evidence for Cărtărescu's sustained quality beyond the best-known volumes turned out thin, I would move toward Carson or Adonis.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first for an unusually distinctive voice and a sustained reconfiguration of genre. She ranks Cărtărescu second, but notes that his very long recursive books may exceed what some readers will finish, and that his Romanian wordplay is hard to verify in translation.
responses.response: I take the translation caveat seriously and share it, since it affects any judgment of Cărtărescu's prose texture. I would not treat the length of the books as a literary weakness in itself; the architecture is part of the achievement, and the question is whether it holds up, which I think it does in the Blinding trilogy. I agree with her on Carson's voice and formal inventiveness. Where I differ is on the whole body of work: Nox and Autobiography of Red are signal books, and I am less sure that the many smaller and occasional volumes sustain the same depth, whereas the Cărtărescu project looks cumulative. I also take her point that the book-object elements need careful citation wording, and that is a practical argument for a prose-centered citation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for a decades-long remaking of Arabic poetic language, with essays that extend the poetry's significance. He ranks Cărtărescu fourth, citing uncertainty about how evenly the very long late volumes hold up and about the limited set of translations.
responses.response: I agree that Adonis's formal and linguistic achievement is of the first rank, and I ranked him third for that reason. We differ mainly on assessability. His achievement lies in Arabic prosody, diction and intertextual play, which most of us can judge only through translation, so a citation would rest on secondhand accounts of the very thing that makes the case. Cărtărescu's translation problem is real but I think less total, because much of his force lies in imagery, structure and scale. I also note Olsson's remark that the recent prominence of other Central and Eastern European writers is not a matter of merit. I agree and do not weigh it. On his point about the late volumes, I accept that evenness cannot be confirmed from here and that this is the right test for the case.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for voice and imaginative scale, but asks of Carson whether the whole body of work reaches the sustained depth the will requires or whether part of it is brilliant formal experiment. She also notes that Magris's essayistic mode raises the question of imaginative depth next to scholarship.
responses.response: Her question about Carson is, I think, the decisive one for the poetry-versus-prose comparison, and I would put the same test to Cărtărescu: does density become mere pattern? I think the Blinding trilogy answers it better than a pure formal-experiment reading would allow, but I hold that view with the caution that my coverage of the poetry and early work is incomplete. On Magris, I agree with her framing and keep him at fifth. His erudition and humane breadth are considerable, but the voice does not seem to me to have the formal intensity of the strongest candidates.

responses.point: Carlberg also ranks Cărtărescu first, as the strongest combination of voice, formal achievement and depth, while flagging that large, self-referential works may be unevenly sustained and that the poetry sits only as a secondary strand in the citation.
responses.response: I agree with her on the citation scope: the prose should carry it and the poetry should be secondary, since my knowledge of the poetry in translation is the weakest part of my assessment. I treat her unevenness caution as a live condition on my view, not a formality. Our agreement on ranking is not itself evidence of merit, and I would want the committee to test the late volumes before treating the case as settled.

uncertainties: Romanian prose of this density and rhythm may be substantially altered in translation, and I cannot independently verify translation quality.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early fiction in translation is limited, so the whole-oeuvre judgment is partial.
Whether the very long late novels are evenly sustained, or sometimes repeat a method, cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.

For Adonis, judging Arabic prosody and its subversion through translation is uncertain, and for Carson it is unclear how scholarly and translation work, and book-object forms, should count toward literary achievement.
I have not independently verified any sources and rely on public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records that I was elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg and has long ties to the SvD and DN culture sections and to Prague and Vienna milieus. My own work concerns Central Europe, which touches the Magris entry (B004) thematically, but the profile does not establish a personal connection to any shortlisted writer, and my own practice is context, not evidence of preference.
